extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in logic, philosophy of mathematics, and formal epistemology (interested in Lakatosian methodology and modal/subset-space logic)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal, logic-based account of Lakatos’s Proofs and Refutations methodology: how to represent primitive conjectures, proofs, counterexamples, and the three Lakatosian strategies (monster-barring, exception-barring, lemma-incorporation) using subset-space logic and controlled contraction mappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive conjecture (stage 1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a possibly loose, overly-general statement of the theorem to be investigated (the 'primitive conjecture'). The methodology assumes conjectures may be false in stated generality and are subject to refinement through proofs and counterexamples (see Euler conjecture V − E + F = 2 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as decomposition into subconjectures and lemmas (stage 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (From section 2.1) "Proof (a rough thought experiment or argument, decomposing the primitive conjecture into subconjectures and lemmas)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce a proof/argument that breaks the conjecture into lemmas and subsidiary claims; record the lemmas explicitly because hidden or implicit lemmas are key targets for refutation or incorporation. Example: Cauchy’s proof uses three implicit lemmas (stretching after removing a face, triangulation producing one face per new edge, removal rules for triangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Global counterexamples (stage 3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for counterexamples that directly refute the main conjecture (not merely a lemma). Examples from PR: nested cubes, picture-frame (torus), urchin, cylinder. Global counterexamples indicate the conjecture in its current form is false and prompt domain restriction or reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof re-examined and guilty lemma spotted (stage 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: (From section 2.1) "Proof re-examined. The guilty lemma is spotted. The guilty lemma may have previously remained hidden or may have been misidentified."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterexample emerges, reanalyze the proof to identify which lemma(s) fail (the 'guilty lemma'). Decide whether to revise lemmas, the proof, or the conjecture. This is central to Lakatos’s method: make hidden lemmas explicit and address them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine other proofs for the newly found lemma (stage 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (From section 2.1) "Proofs of the other theorems are examined to see if the newly found lemma occurs in them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the identified lemma appears in other proofs/theorems — i.e., test consequences and dependencies — to assess the impact of modifying or discarding that lemma across the body of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check previously accepted consequences (stage 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: (From section 2.1) "Hitherto accepted consequences of the original and now refuted conjecture are checked."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit accepted corollaries and consequences of the original conjecture for consistency with any proposed revisions; ensure downstream results remain valid or are appropriately revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn counterexamples into new examples / open new inquiry (stage 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: (From section 2.1) "Counterexamples are turned into new examples, and new fields of inquiry open up."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat counterexamples as sources of new concepts and new conjectures (e.g., torus leading to genus); transform 'monsters' into legitimate examples for modified conjectures, thereby expanding mathematical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring (strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.1) "The method of 'monster-barring' deals with the objects which are not in mind when the conjecture is put forward. They are, in this sense, monsters and should be excluded from our domain of discourse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude pathological or unintended cases from the domain by refining definitions so that the conjecture holds for the intended class (e.g., restrict to 'simple' polyhedra). Guidance/anti-patterns: beware of abusing monster-barring as a mere linguistic trick to rescue a conjecture — distinguish legitimate domain restriction from ad hoc exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring (strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.1 and Appendix) "Exception-barring accepts that the theorem in its stated form is not valid due to the emergence of some genuine counterexamples ... these counterexamples should be excluded from the original domain which results in a contraction of the domain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract the domain by identifying and excluding exceptions via explicit restrictive clauses, thereby improving the conjecture (e.g., restrict to convex polyhedra). Guidance: prefer precise delimitation of domain over cavalier dismissal of counterexamples as monsters; exception-barring is for finding the domain where the formula is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma incorporation (strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.1 and Appendix) "Lemma incorporation describes ... how we turn the counterexamples into new examples, and those new examples are helpful for the modified and reformulated version of the theorem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate additional lemmas/conditions discovered via counterexamples into the statement of the theorem (e.g., introduce genus g(x) and reformulate Euler’s formula as V − E + F = 2 − 2·g(x)). This upholds the proof by making implicit lemmas explicit and part of the theorem’s hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between local and global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 3/4 and Appendix) "Local counterexamples deny the specific lemmas or the constructions which were used in the proof without targeting the main conjecture itself. However, global counterexamples deny the main conjecture, and without even consulting the proof, demonstrate that the conjecture is false."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify counterexamples to decide response: local counterexamples suggest fixing lemmas or constructions; global counterexamples require revising the conjecture (or its domain). Examples: local counterexample targets a lemma in the proof; global counterexample like the picture-frame contradicts the main claim directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive vs negative heuristic roles of counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 2.2) "Positive heuristic contains rules that help us in application, in the formation of a fallible version of the hard core [of the theorem]... The role of negative heuristic is simply to defend the hard core maybe in a less creative way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate counterexamples by their heuristic role: use positive heuristics to generate constructive rules and reforms; negative heuristics serve to protect core assumptions. Recognize that the same counterexample can have mixed (ambiguous) heuristic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not uncritically dismiss counterexamples as monsters
rubrics_metrics.description: (Appendix quotations and discussion) Critics may call a counterexample 'a monster' to reject it, but Lakatosian method requires examination rather than immediate dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-pattern of reflexive rejection of counterexamples (Delta's 'monster' move). Instead, analyse whether the counterexample reveals hidden lemmas, signals domain mis-specification, or should be turned into new examples/fields (Beta’s approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule I — Proof-analysis and search for counterexamples (Appendix)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Appendix) "Rule I. If you have a conjecture, set out to prove it and to refute it. Inspect the proof carefully to prepare a list of non-trivial lemmas (proof-analysis); find counterexamples both to the conjecture (global counterexamples) and to the suspect lemmas (local counterexamples)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively pursue both proof construction and refutation; produce explicit proof-analysis (list lemmas) as a diagnostic tool. Scoring/quality: a good methodological practice documents lemmas and seeks counterexamples systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule II — Responding to global counterexamples (Appendix)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Appendix) "Rule 2. If you have a global counterexample discard your conjecture, add to your proof-analysis a suitable lemma that will be refuted by it, and replace the discarded conjecture by an improved one that incorporates that lemma as a condition. Do not allow a refutation to be dismissed as a monster. Make all 'hidden lemmas' explicit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a global counterexample is found, reformulate the conjecture to incorporate the condition (lemma) that rescues (or explains) the proof; make explicit what was previously implicit. Anti-pattern: allowing dismissal of a counterexample without substantive revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule III — Handling local counterexamples (Appendix)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Appendix) "Rule 3. If you have a local counterexample, check to see whether it is not also a global counterexample. If it is, you can easily apply Rule 2."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat local counterexamples as pointers: check whether they generalize to global counterexamples; if so, apply Rule II (reformulate). Otherwise, use them to refine lemmas or constructions used in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order/sequence sensitivity of methodological steps
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 4.1) "consecutive and ordered application of a variety of, say, counterexamples, can be captured in this framework as it is not necessarily the case that f(g(U)) = g(f(U)) for contracting mappings f and g. Therefore, the order of the application of contracting mappings matters..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing heuristic updates (e.g., via contraction mappings or successive domain restrictions), preserve the order of methodological steps — different sequences of exclusions/lemmas can lead to different outcomes. Methodologically, document the order in which counterexamples/adjustments are applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization requirement: represent epistemic methods as contraction mappings (controlled subset spaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 3.2 and 4.1) Introduce controlled subset spaces with a set F of contraction mappings (epistemic methods), and represent controlled shrinking by a modality [F] so that applying f in F yields the subdomain of objects satisfying a candidate conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing Lakatosian heuristics, explicitly model the 'effort' or method of restricting possibilities: define contraction mappings f whose images f(U) capture the objects verified by a testing/probing procedure (e.g., f returns only objects with Euler characteristic 2). Use [F] and its dual hF i to capture universal/existential controlled shrinkings. Guidance: ensure f are contraction mappings (f(U) ⊆ U) and require s ∈ f(U) to keep neighborhood situations meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish verification from discovery (limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Section 4.5) The formal model focuses on verification (selecting and verifying functions/methods that work) rather than on how new concepts or lemmas are originally discovered; concept-generation is practice-based and not captured by the formal framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the methodological limitation: formal/algorithmic frameworks can represent testing, verification, and reformulation of conjectures, but they do not predict or generate novel conceptual inventions (e.g., introduction of genus). Use the formalism descriptively rather than as a full model of discovery.
